mishnah-berurah/part-001.txt.2:ז: (13) The one who blesses etc.—for since he discharges his fellows with the zimun blessing it is stricter.
mishnah-berurah/part-001.txt.2:ח: (14) Vegetable—and the same applies to any beverage, as above.
mishnah-berurah/part-001.txt.3:א: (15) He must bless—after he finishes hearing the zimun blessing.
mishnah-berurah/part-001.txt.3:ב: (16) And he is not discharged—meaning even if he wishes to intend to be discharged by birkat hamazon it does not help, as we hold [below siman 208 seif 17 and Acharonim there] that the blessing of three does not discharge the category of three, nor Borei nefashot rabot; but if he ate dates or drank wine it certainly helps b'dieved, for we hold in siman 208 that if b'dieved he blessed on them in birkat hamazon he fulfilled; and per what several Acharonim ruled there—even for porridge, if he blessed in birkat hamazon he fulfilled—also for porridge the law is thus; and Magen Avraham wrote nevertheless l'chatchila he should intend with them not to be discharged by birkat hamazon, for he must bless on every species its fitting blessing.
mishnah-berurah/part-001.txt.3:ג: (17) To join for ten—for without him there is an obligation of zimun from the bread-eaters, and we do not need him except for mention of the Name.
mishnah-berurah/part-001.txt.3:ד: (18) Kazayit of bread—for he is obligated in birkat hamazon.
mishnah-berurah/part-001.txt.3:ה: (19) That with a kazayit of grain etc.—meaning such as porridge and the like from types of food one must bless on them one blessing of the category of three.
mishnah-berurah/part-001.txt.3:ו: (20) That with vegetables and any food—and the same applies to drinking; and as above in seif 2 regarding ten; and the reason for this view is that for joining zimun they are lenient also for three, since two of them ate bread and are obligated in birkat hamazon, and the third ate a kazayit he is at least obligated in a final blessing.
mishnah-berurah/part-001.txt.3:ז: (21) Therefore two etc.—this is the Mechaber's words to decide between the views: l'chatchila they should urge him to eat bread specifically to fulfill the first view; and if he does not want they should not give him anything so as not to enter themselves into doubt of obligation; but b'dieved if it happened they gave him something that is not bread—they must be concerned for the second view and invite zimun with him.
mishnah-berurah/part-001.txt.3:ח: (22) To drink—and now the custom is if he does not want to eat bread they give him l'chatchila to drink or to eat something, per the other view [Acharonim].
mishnah-berurah/part-001.txt.4:א: (23) Mitzvah etc.—for since many of them ate to satiety and are obligated in birkat hamazon from the Torah, it is better he discharge them also—he who ate to satiety and is obligated from the Torah like them. Acharonim wrote all this if he discharges them in birkat hamazon; but if each blesses by himself and only one invites zimun upon them—we are not so strict; and l'chatchila one can invite zimun upon them even one who did not eat except a kazayit.
mishnah-berurah/part-001.txt.4:ב: (24) He can discharge etc.—for from the Torah he can discharge his fellow in birkat hamazon even though he did not eat at all, since his fellow already ate and is obligated to bless and all Israel are guarantors for one another; except because he speaks falsely in saying "who has fed us" when he did not eat, the Sages required he eat a kazayit first; and see Magen Avraham who is uncertain that per this, if they are only two—for otherwise they do not invite zimun—it is possible he can discharge his fellow who does not know how to bless even if he did not eat at all; and he sides to be strict; and so in Eliyah Rabbah—that d'rabbanan in all cases one does not discharge his fellow in birkat hamazon unless he too is obligated in the matter; and so is proven explicitly in Chiddushei HaRa'ah to Berachot and Ritva Rosh Hashanah 29, and in Shitah Mekubetzet Berachot 48—see there.
mishnah-berurah/part-001.txt.4:ג: (25) Some say he is not obligated etc.—for they hold that what R' Meir expounds in the gemara "and you shall eat" refers to eating and "and you were satisfied" refers to drinking—meaning if he drank after eating then he is obligated to bless, and if not he is not obligated except d'rabbanan.
mishnah-berurah/part-001.txt.4:ד: (26) And he is thirsty to drink—for if he is not thirsty to drink, for everyone he is obligated d'oraisa even without drinking.
mishnah-berurah/part-001.txt.4:ה: (27) And it is good to be careful l'chatchila—meaning per Shulchan Aruch's ruling above that if there is one obligated in the matter d'oraisa who knows how to bless, it is a mitzvah he bless to discharge others; it is good to be concerned also for this view that one who drank after his eating bless to discharge others, for he is certainly obligated d'oraisa—unless those who drank do not know how to bless, then one who did not drink can discharge them, as the Mechaber also wrote regarding satiety.
mishnah-berurah/part-001.txt.4:ו: (28) That one who drank bless—and nevertheless if some ate to satiety and did not drink, and some did not eat to satiety and drank—it is better they bless over those who ate to satiety, for they are obligated d'oraisa per the poskim even if they did not drink; and Mordechai's view in the name of Ra'avan is a lone view. One who was satiated before he ate and ate coarse eating he did not need—nevertheless if his throat enjoyed that eating he blesses before and after it and discharges others; and if his soul was disgusted by it and his throat did not enjoy it, he is not fit to bless neither before nor after it, for this is not considered eating at all for any mitzvah in the Torah, as explained in siman 476 and siman 612.

peri-megadim/part-001.txt.1:א: All. Taz in siman 196 ot 2 challenged: why Kohen and non-Kohen with gentile bread do not combine, and in Eliyah Rabbah 196 ot 3 he answered somewhat—see there; and ostensibly it implies they can eat even though they are not desirous; and see Levush and Perishah. But if they are so satiated they cannot eat at all, he does not combine. And know: if they finished their meal and a third came—if they said explicitly they do not wish to fix a meal, then there is no zimun, even though they do not act properly, for they are obligated to return after zimun as in siman 193; but if they were silent and the third came and ate a kazayit, they are obligated, for it is fixing a meal; and what is written in 193 seif 2 that they are fixed at finishing the meal—this too is included, since they can eat; and so Rashi Berachot 47a s.v. akilna: "you do not obligate us in zimun"—and he was forced to explain thus, for Rav in 45b holds two—it is optional to invite; and if it were R' Shimon bar Yochai also with them to say the zimun blessing, alternatively he does not combine—he can answer "Blessed are You... who has fed us from His bounty," as Rashi 45b explained "he came and found them"—since he did not eat; and see siman 198 in Magen Avraham 1 (and to discharge himself with their birkat hamazon R' Shimon bar Yochai would not protest for this)—it teaches obligation of zimun for all of them, and great is the mitzvah etc.; and it is difficult for Maharal who holds all who were not fixed with haMotzi are not obligated—see siman 193 in Tur from here; and Orach Mishpat chapter 5 of Berachot halacha 9 wrote: and a third came and ate etc.—obligated in zimun; and in Shulchan Aruch he wrote l'chatchila; and from Kohen and non-Kohen one can say it is as if they said explicitly they do not wish to fix a meal—unlike here where they were silent; and all this in our innovations there.
peri-megadim/part-001.txt.1:ב: In Eliyah Rabbah 4—he is uncertain if when one can eat and the other cannot, whether they combine; and practical difference: if one said "hav venevarekh"—see there. And I am uncertain whether we require he can eat specifically a kazayit or anything at all; and Orach Mishpat chapter 5 halacha 9—even anything at all, and even from other foods—one can say all the more so other foods is meant. Also what is written "they can eat" and not "they can drink" requires study.
peri-megadim/part-001.txt.2:_: The one who joins. Taz l'chatchila; also Magen Avraham 7 concedes it is fitting to bless a blessing of the category of three on wine and dates, and b'dieved he is exempt. And Magen Avraham 177:16—there it is b'dieved, for he eats dates after the meal and has birkat hamazon before him—he is exempt even l'chatchila like wine; however in chapter 182 Magen Avraham 8-9 it does not imply thus—see there in Pri Megadim.
peri-megadim/part-001.txt.3:_: He can. Taz; Tosafot Berachot 48a s.v. until—see there; and Rosh Hashanah 29a; and Magen Avraham 11 that two and one—a Torah scholar blesses even if he did not eat at all. Levush in his commentary brought Yerushalmi that Beit Yosef brought: "and you shall eat and bless"—one who ate blesses; and those who wish to benefit bless—if so there is no place in birkat hamazon that one does not bless unless like a kazayit of grain; even Borei nefashot rabot one does not discharge unless he ate, as we hold such too does not help and he should not bless even though he already ate and is obligated—nevertheless those who wish to benefit apply, and he had no need to eat unless he learned the blessings—see siman 196 Magen Avraham ot 40; and here ot 11; and in Levush he wrote kazayit of bread specifically, not porridge—and if so it will be explained further in Magen Avraham.
peri-megadim/part-001.txt.4:_: If. Taz—behold we hold eating to satiety, then he is obligated—45, and 184:66 and 186:62; and there are poskim like R' Meir with kazayit and "and you were satisfied" refers to drinking; and there is leniency and stringency for each of the explanations; therefore Rama wrote it is good; and nevertheless the essence is as those who say satiety, and he need not drink; and Magen Avraham 11 and Mordechai—it is possible he holds in such a case one obligated d'rabbanan does not discharge d'oraisa, for guarantors apply only to what one is obligated in, and one cannot be exempt from it—unlike optional eating; and nevertheless for us d'rabbanan discharges d'oraisa because of guarantors, as written in ot 3; and therefore only good from two aspects—and one should not elaborate.

shaarei-teshuvah/part-001.txt.1:_: With them—see Baer Heitev. And see Eliyah Rabbah who wrote there is no root and meaning in Talmud and poskim that there should be a mitzvah to return and eat; and it is reasonable this is like coarse eating etc.—see there; and see Birkei Yosef in the name of responsum Sha'arei Yeshu'a manuscript 9 "they ate"—they thought they were ten and took mayim acharonim and gave the cup to bless and saw they were only nine—it does not help to add one by giving him to drink in order to bless with the Name, just as it does not help for zimun of three—see there.
shaarei-teshuvah/part-001.txt.2:_: They combine—see Baer Heitev and what I wrote in my responsum above siman 194 on this matter.
shaarei-teshuvah/part-001.txt.4:_: Water—see Baer Heitev and what Eliyah Rabbah wrote in Shibolei Leket that one who drank a majority of a revi'it combines—he did not find a colleague among poskim.

turei-zahav/part-001.txt.1:_: Wherever etc. In the previous siman I challenged from this—see there.
turei-zahav/part-001.txt.2:_: The one who joins must bless etc.—for birkat hamazon does not discharge Borei nefashot rabot, nor a blessing of the category of three; and Shimon ben Shetach who was drinking a cup of wine and blessed for King Yannai—even in this we say he did for himself, for he holds Borei nefashot rabot discharges the category of three etc., as explained in Beit Yosef in the name of Rashba.
turei-zahav/part-001.txt.3:_: He can discharge even those etc.—and even though this one who ate a kazayit is obligated only d'rabbanan, for d'oraisa we require actual satiety as I wrote "and you were satisfied and bless"—nevertheless this one can discharge others, for all Israel are guarantors for one another, as we say in chapter "they saw him" in court—all blessings, even if he fulfilled he discharges, and he need not eat a kazayit of grain but that he can say "who has fed us from His bounty"—so Tosafot and Rosh chapter "three who ate."
turei-zahav/part-001.txt.4:_: If he did not drink and he is thirsty to drink. So Beit Yosef in the name of Mordechai; and his reason: since we hold like R' Meir who said "and you were satisfied" refers to drinking—if so he is not obligated d'oraisa unless he drank if he needs to drink etc.; therefore one who ate and did not drink cannot discharge others with it, for the Sages do not come and produce d'oraisa from this; and Beit Yosef challenged this, for Tosafot chapter "three who ate" wrote the verses are merely asmakhta; and further—even per those who hold the verses are not asmakhta but kazayit is d'oraisa—from where do we know birkat eating depends on drinking—perhaps the verse means when you eat or drink you bless Hashem your God; and so all poskim who did not write this, and so we rule that even if he desires to drink he discharges others with it—end of his words; therefore Rama wrote it is good to be careful l'chatchila etc.; and in my humble opinion it is difficult on Mordechai's words—why can he not discharge others without drinking, for we already said nearby that even if he did not eat at all he can discharge others in this mitzvah, except we require a kazayit of grain so he can say "who has fed us"—and here he can well say "who has fed us," even though he is not obligated in Borei nefashot rabot per one view since he did not drink—nevertheless he is within "who has fed us" and can discharge others who drank because of guarantors as written nearby; and if you say he cannot say "who has fed us" since he did not drink—if so it should have said "who has fed us and given us drink," the language of Scripture that mentioned drinking separately and not within "and you shall eat."

yad-ephraim/part-001.txt.1:_: In Taz s.k. 2—for King Yannai; and perhaps Shimon ben Shetach also in this did for himself, for he holds birkat hamazon discharges the category of three; or alternatively wine is different, for wine does zimun etc.—thus is the reading; and so in Chiddushei Rashba that he brought—see there.
